cards.b:
Hotspots, endemic species, invasive plants and the global biodiversity framework come up often in Prelims. Mains uses them in questions on conservation, climate and development.

India holds about 2.4 percent of Earth’s land and a much larger share (roughly 7 to 8 percent) of known species. It is one of the megadiverse countries.

Genetic diversity: variation within a species, such as thousands of rice varieties. Species diversity: the number and spread of species. Ecosystem diversity: variety of habitats like forests, wetlands and deserts.

Whittaker split species diversity into alpha (within a habitat), beta (between habitats) and gamma (across a region).

Diversity rises toward the equator. This is the latitudinal gradient: tropical regions have more stable climate, more energy and a longer evolutionary history.

The species-area relationship (Humboldt) says larger areas hold more species. The equation S = CA^Z gives a slope (Z) of about 0.1 to 0.2 on regional scales. This is why habitat fragmentation matters.

Norman Myers (1988) proposed biodiversity hotspots. Conservation International now uses two tests: at least 1,500 endemic vascular plant species and at least 70 percent of original habitat lost. There are about 36 hotspots worldwide.

They cover a small fraction of land but hold a very large share of endemic plants and vertebrates.

• Himalaya: the whole range, including Bhutan, Nepal and parts of Tibet.
  • Indo-Burma: North-East India south of the Brahmaputra, plus Myanmar and more.
  • Western Ghats and Sri Lanka: very high endemism.
  • Sundaland: in India, only the Nicobar Islands.

Hotspots are defined by Norman Myers' criteria: at least 1,500 endemic vascular plant species and loss of at least 70 percent of original habitat. The Eastern Himalaya part is rich in orchids and rhododendrons, and the Western Ghats hold many amphibians. India's Indo-Burma portion includes Manipur, Mizoram and Nagaland, and the Nicobar Islands form its Sundaland part.

Jared Diamond called the main causes the “evil quartet”: habitat loss and fragmentation, overexploitation, alien species invasion and co-extinction. Climate change and pollution are now added.

Habitat loss is the top cause. Poaching, the wildlife trade and human-animal conflict add pressure.

Habitat loss includes clearing for farms, mines, dams and roads, and also fragmentation, which splits a large habitat into patches too small for wide-ranging animals such as elephants and tigers. Edge effects then make the remaining patches poorer. Co-extinction means a species dies because its partner does, such as a parasite that depends on one host. The Millennium Ecosystem Assessment (2005) also named climate change, pollution and overexploitation among the main drivers.

India’s major invasives include Lantana camara, water hyacinth, Prosopis juliflora, Parthenium and Chromolaena. They crowd out native plants and reduce grazing and water.

The Wildlife (Protection) Amendment Act 2022 gave the Centre power to regulate invasive alien species. Control costs are high, and removal programmes in tiger reserves such as Bandipur and Mudumalai are ongoing.

Invasives spread through trade, travel and deliberate introduction. Water hyacinth, native to South America, was brought as an ornamental plant and now chokes ponds and lakes, cutting oxygen for fish. Lantana came from tropical America in the colonial period as a garden shrub and now covers large forest areas. Alien species often lack natural predators in the new home, which is why they spread fast. The Convention on Biological Diversity (Article 8h) asks countries to prevent and control them.

The Convention on Biological Diversity (Rio, 1992) set the base. In December 2022 at COP15 (Montreal), nations adopted the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework with 23 targets for 2030.

Key targets: protect 30 percent of land and sea by 2030 (“30 by 30”), restore 30 percent of degraded areas, and mobilise about $200 billion a year from all sources. Developed countries are to give $20 billion a year in international finance by 2025 and $30 billion by 2030.

The Biological Diversity Act 2002 set up the National Biodiversity Authority (Chennai, 2003), State Biodiversity Boards and local Biodiversity Management Committees. It covers access and benefit sharing, based on the Nagoya Protocol.

The Biological Diversity (Amendment) Act 2023 eased rules for AYUSH users and decriminalised some offences. India released an updated National Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan with national targets in line with the Kunming-Montreal framework (as of 2024).

CBD COP17 was due in Armenia in late 2026; check its outcome before the exam.

Mains-style: “What are biodiversity hotspots? Why is the Western Ghats a hotspot, and what threatens it?” Structure: definition and two criteria; Western Ghats endemism; threats (mining, plantations, tourism, landslides); Gadgil and Kasturirangan reports; remedies.

Mains-style: “Invasive alien species are a silent threat to Indian ecosystems. Discuss.”

Prelims tip: Remember the two hotspot criteria numbers (1,500 and 70 percent). India’s hotspot in the Nicobar Islands belongs to Sundaland.

quiz.q: The two criteria for a hotspot include losing what share of original habitat?
quiz.w: Conservation International: 1,500 endemic plants and 70 percent habitat lost.

quiz.q: Which of these is not an Indian hotspot?
quiz.w: Only the Nicobar Islands part of Sundaland is in India, so Sundaland as a whole is not.

quiz.q: Who proposed the hotspot concept in 1988?
quiz.w: Myers proposed it; Conservation International later refined it.
Alpha is within a habitat, beta is between, gamma is regional.

quiz.q: Which is an invasive plant in India?
quiz.w: Lantana was introduced and now spreads through many forests.

quiz.q: The Kunming-Montreal framework aims to protect what share of land and sea by 2030?
quiz.w: This is the “30 by 30” target adopted in 2022.

quiz.q: The National Biodiversity Authority is headquartered at:
quiz.w: NBA was set up in 2003 at Chennai under the 2002 Act.

quiz.q: Which Act deals with access and benefit sharing in India?
quiz.w: The BD Act implements the benefit sharing idea of CBD and the Nagoya Protocol.

o: Extinction of all species in a hotspot
A species dies because a partner species died
quiz.w: Example: a parasite or pollinator lost with its host.
